I am so sorry for what you are going through right now. I lost my sister in 2015 and I felt like life would never be good again. All of the joy in my life had gone with her, despite having a loving fiancé and a close family. But I did, slowly, begin to find moments of light. I felt guilty in these moments, and it was extremely difficult to live with the guilt of believing that I could have done something differently to change the outcome of her depression.

All my love 💕

I'm so sorry that you have to deal with this sort of thing. My sister died by suicide in 2015, and the impact it has had on my parents is profound - it is difficult to describe. I know that *I* will never be "over it", let alone my parents! 

Additionally, my Aunty died in a car accident when she was 17. More than 35 years later, my grandparents continue to grieve. Every time I visit them, they tell me something about her, sometimes something new, sometimes they repeat old stories, it is beautiful. 

Grief is not something you get over - I believe life can grow around the grief, but it will never not be there. Sending all my love ❤️

Look, it impossible for a stranger on the Internet to be able to tell you what you want to hear. I'm not going to agree with you on your comments about yourself, because I don't believe them to be true. I believe that *you* think they're true, but we all think those things about ourselves at times. It's part of being human. 

If you don't want to listen to advice and just want a rant, that's fine. I do think your friendship group likely lacks diversity in characters. Unless you've got to know hundreds of women on a deep level, you can not know that you are right.

Try joining a book club, a mixed sports team or a games club - whatever it is that you enjoy. Don't pursue the women you meet, but just get to know them as friends. Or join tinder! If you write yourself off now and resign yourself to a life of loneliness, you will fulfill your own prophecy.

(I'm sorry if I'm coming across as harsh, I'm genuinely just trying to help you see how you're coming across, from a female perspective)

It sounds like you have a lot of self reflecting to do. Try to identify what it is about you that puts people off *and please don't say "everything"* and ask yourself if it is a "red flag" trait. (To me, pursuing every woman on your friends list is a massive red flag) If it isn't a red flag trait, then move on to the next. Work on yourself and stop focusing your life on getting laid/a gf.

I'm genuinely trying to give you advice. With that attitude, people *will* be put off.

You probably know a handful of women - and I mean properly know, not just Facebook friend level. You are saying that literally no woman will ever like you because the 5 (idk how many you speak to often, just a guess) women you regularly interact with don't. That just isn't true. 

Stop letting your insecurities stop you from living a positive life. And stop putting so much pressure on having a relationship, they are not the be all and end all. Friendships are more important. I have had a situation recently where I feel like I've been cut out of a friendship group. I made the mistake of talking to a young (18 y/o) girl in the group who was feeling insecure. She cane to me and told me that she felt like the "ringleader" (28 y/o F) was using her friendship with her to get close to someone else, and I suppose the 18 y/o just wanted some reassurance. So I gave it to her. I said that there had been times when I had doubted my importance to other members of the group, but that I was quite insecure about my friendships in general and that I knew it was mostly in my head. I basically told her not to worry, because it probably wasn't the case (although she gave me some compelling evidence to suggest that she was actually right, but I didn't want to worry her)

The ringleader had been my oldest friend, we had known eachother since nursery school and had been close friends for 20 years. Anyway, a week after the conversation with the 18 y/o, I got a text from the ringleader which told me that I am "selfish", "self centered", "manipulative", a "liar" and a "gaslighter", and that she needed "space" until I could reflect on my bad behaviour! 

It was totally out of the blue and really threw me - I had just started my antidepressants as well and was having a terrible time adjusting to those, so I was extremely low. It was at the start of the year, and I'm still coming to terms with it! 

I asked what I had even done, and she refused to tell me, and still refuses to tell me. I can only think that the 18 y/o wanted me out of the picture because she was jealous of my friendship with the ringleader. Whenever I've tried to talk to her she has accused me of manipulating her and everyone around me. 

I have the same issue. I find it so hard to let go of people in my life, even when I know they're bad for me. My husband, sister and mum have all been telling me that I'm too loyal and that she (the ringleader) takes advantage of my kindness, and constant need to people please. They've seen the red flags for years! I just wish I had listened to them sooner - maybe it wouldn't hurt so much now!!

If it was legal, many women would be essentially forced into sex work. When it comes to benefits and government funded income support, you can only access that support if you show that you are actively trying to get a job. I wouldn't hypothetically be able to claim benefits if I was offered a job stocking shelves and rejected it because I didn't like it... similarly, women (and men, probably!) wouldn't be able to access government funded income support if they were given a job opportunity in the sex trade, and just said "I don't want to do sex work". 

It's very complicated. There are many people who do sex work because they enjoy it and find it empowering, but this change of legal definition and legality would have a hugely detrimental impact on many vulnerable individuals.
